Q: Filter out rows from a DataFrame if value in columns X and Y match MultiIndex A and B A:

You can first turn the ["TEST", "RECORDING"] columns of A into a pd.Index using .set_index, then use pd.Index.isin to find a mask representing the rows whose (TEST, RECORDING) pairs are in B.index, then negate the mask and index back A.

In short:

C = A[~A.set_index(["TEST", "RECORDING"]).index.isin(B.index)]

Output:

   TEST  RECORDING   FILENAME
4     3          1  ghjk.xlsx
5     3          2  vbnm.xlsx

Setup:

import pandas as pd

A = pd.DataFrame(
    {"TEST": [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3],
     "RECORDING": [1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2],
     "FILENAME": ["qwer.xlsx", "asdf.xlsx", "zxcv.xlsx", "tyui.xlsx", "ghjk.xlsx", "vbnm.xlsx"]})

B = pd.DataFrame(
    {"STARTS": [1, 1, 2, 2],
     "ERRORS": [0, 0, 0, 0],
     "START RUN TIME": [0, 10, 20, 30],
     "END RUN TIME": [5, 15, 25, 35]},
    index=pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples([(1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 2)], names=["Test", "Rec"]))

Q: How to boot up from CDROM (ISO image) to install the guest OS using virsh A:

Thanks for DanielB's help! The '--debug' argument of virt-install does reveal the information I need to solve this problem.

First of all, in the XML definition, I don't need the <loader> line. The <os> section should be:

<os>
  <type arch='x86_64' machine='pc-i440fx-trusty'>hvm</type>
  <boot dev='cdrom'/>
  <boot dev='hd'/>
</os>

The two <boot> tags already specify the order of booting.

Secondly, virt-install's debug output suggests the desired way to bring up virt-viewer:

  • Run: virt-viewer --connect=qemu:///system --wait vm_c2
    • Optionally, you can add '--debug' and '--verbose' to virt-viewer to see more output.
    • At this moment, the viewer window should be brought up and a message is shown: Waiting for guest domain to be created.
  • Run: virsh create --file def_domain_test.xml.
    • The viewer would now be activated and display the output of the VM.

Here is one caveat which caused me to get stuck at the beginning: You don't have to start virt-viewer prior to the VM. However, if you start VM first and then the viewer, the viewer screen may be a whole black one which may confuse you and make you think nothing is happening there. In this case, click the viewer window to let it get the input focus, then press 'Enter' key and you may get it refreshed and see what is there actually. (Resizing the window doesn't force it to refresh.)

FYI: If you output the virt-viewer's debug messages, you may see a message like this:

(virt-viewer:6296): virt-viewer-DEBUG: Error operation forbidden: read only access prevents virDomainOpenGraphics

This doesn't seem to cause me any problems, but maybe it's the hint of other problems if virt-viewer doesn't work correctly for you.

Q: Can't access localhost with vagrant port forwarding A:

TL;DR

There seems to be a bug in vagrant, where vagrant destroy doesn't get rid of old port forwarding, so you need to kill it manually, and then re-run vagrant up

Details...

I'm running into what I think is probably the same problem, and here's what I'm finding:

It seems that vagrant destroy (optionally with -f) doesn't stop the process that gets started to do port forwarding, which I'm finding to remain running, like so (edited to elide some details, and make it multi-line for easier reading):

: PROMPT$; ps -ft `tty` www
lindes    393307    4880  0 15:27 pts/9    S      0:00 \
    ssh -n -o User=vagrant -o Port=22 -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null \
    -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -o ControlMaster=no \
    -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o PasswordAuthentication=no \
    -o ForwardX11=no -o IdentitiesOnly=yes \
    -o IdentityFile=".vagrant/machines/default/libvirt/private_key" \
    -L *:8080:192.168.121.199:80 -N 192.168.121.199

But that's not the address currently in use:

: PROMPT$; vagrant ssh -c 'ip addr' |grep 192|cut -d/ -f1|awk '{print $2}'
192.168.121.251

So, the port forwarding process lingers around with a stale IP address, it seems. If I kill that ssh process, though, and then run vagrant halt; vagrant up, then it properly gets re-started, with matching IP addresses, as evidenced here:

: PROMPT$; ps -ft `tty` www | grep ssh | sed -ne 's/.*-L/-L/p' | uniq
-L *:8080:192.168.121.251:80 -N 192.168.121.251
: PROMPT$; vagrant ssh -c 'ip addr' |grep 192|cut -d/ -f1 |awk '{print $2}' 
192.168.121.251

And indeed, when it's in sync, it seems that vagrant halt will actually kill the ssh process, and so regardless of what address it gets next time, it'll re-start the fowarding:

: PROMPT$; ps -ft `tty` www | grep ssh | sed -ne 's/.*-L/-L/p' | uniq
-L *:8081:192.168.121.180:80 -N 192.168.121.180
: PROMPT$; vagrant ssh -c 'ip addr' |grep 192|cut -d/ -f1 |awk '{print $2}'
192.168.121.180
: PROMPT$; vagrant halt 
==> default: Clearing any previously set forwarded ports...
==> default: Attempting graceful shutdown of VM...
: PROMPT$; ps -ft `tty` www | grep ssh | sed -ne 's/.*-L/-L/p' | uniq      
: PROMPT$; 
: PROMPT$; vagrant up
Bringing machine 'default' up with 'libvirt' provider...
==> default: Checking if box 'debian/trixie64' version '13.20260519.1' is up to date...
==> default: Starting domain.
==> default: Waiting for domain to get an IP address...
==> default: Waiting for machine to boot. This may take a few minutes...
    default: SSH address: 192.168.121.180:22
    default: SSH username: vagrant
    default: SSH auth method: private key
==> default: Machine booted and ready!
==> default: Creating shared folders metadata...
==> default: Forwarding ports...
==> default: 80 (guest) => 8081 (host) (adapter eth0)
==> default: Rsyncing folder: /home/lindes/src/test/pandoc/ => /vagrant
==> default: Machine already provisioned. Run `vagrant provision` or use the `--provision`
==> default: flag to force provisioning. Provisioners marked to run always will still run.

==> default: Machine 'default' has a post `vagrant up` message. This is a message
==> default: from the creator of the Vagrantfile, and not from Vagrant itself:
==> default: 
==> default: Vanilla Debian box. See https://app.vagrantup.com/debian for help and bug reports
: PROMPT$; ps -ft `tty` www | grep ssh | sed -ne 's/.*-L/-L/p' | uniq
-L *:8081:192.168.121.180:80 -N 192.168.121.180
: PROMPT$; vagrant ssh -c 'ip addr' |grep 192|cut -d/ -f1 |awk '{print $2}'
192.168.121.180
: PROMPT$;

But if I do vagrant destroy (as I often will do repeatedly when developing provisioning scripts, to ensure they're properly working from a blank slate), it gets out of sync, and once it is, then whether I halt or destroy again, either way, the forwarder ssh process lingers from the old address, and re-start (or destroy and start) without killing the process, leaves things out of whack:

: PROMPT$; ps -ft `tty` www | grep ssh | sed -ne 's/.*-L/-L/p' | uniq
-L *:8081:192.168.121.180:80 -N 192.168.121.180
: PROMPT$; vagrant ssh -c 'ip addr' |grep 192|cut -d/ -f1 |awk '{print $2}'
192.168.121.180
: PROMPT$; 
: PROMPT$; 
: PROMPT$; vagrant destroy -f
==> default: Clearing any previously set forwarded ports...
==> default: Removing domain...
==> default: Deleting the machine folder
: PROMPT$; ps -ft `tty` www | grep ssh | sed -ne 's/.*-L/-L/p' | uniq
-L *:8081:192.168.121.180:80 -N 192.168.121.180
: PROMPT$; vagrant up

: PROMPT$;
: PROMPT$; ps -ft `tty` www | grep ssh | sed -ne 's/.*-L/-L/p' | uniq
-L *:8081:192.168.121.180:80 -N 192.168.121.180
: PROMPT$; vagrant ssh -c 'ip addr' |grep 192|cut -d/ -f1 |awk '{print $2}'
192.168.121.240
: PROMPT$;

Seems like a bug... so, I've submitted an issue on it.

But bottom line, find and kill the ssh process, and re-run vagrant up (after either vagrant halt or vagrant destroy), and you should be good to go again.
